c.tagline: Sacred city holy to three faiths

taxi.fareNote: meter (moneh) required by law; insist it is used

emergency.note: Fire is 102; 112 also works from mobile phones, and English-speaking operators are common.

hood_landmark.Old City: The Western Wall and Church of the Holy Sepulchre within its four walled quarters
hood_landmark.German Colony: Emek Refaim Street's cafes lined with 19th-century Templer architecture
hood_landmark.Rehavia: Jason's Tomb, a Hasmonean-era rock-cut tomb amid leafy streets
hood_landmark.Mea Shearim: Its preserved 19th-century ultra-Orthodox courtyards and Yiddish-speaking street life
hood_landmark.Nachlaot: The adjacent Machane Yehuda Market and a maze of picturesque stone lanes

avoid.reason: Tourist areas safe; tension and occasional unrest in the Old City (esp. around holy sites on Fridays/holidays) and East Jerusalem — avoid protests and flashpoints

hood_desc: The walled ancient heart with the Western Wall, Church of the Holy Sepulchre, Dome of the Rock and Al-Aqsa and the four quarters; suits pilgrims and history seekers wanting to be inside the sacred core.
An elegant, leafy district of restored Templer stone houses along Emek Refaim with cafes and boutiques; suits travelers wanting an upscale, walkable, atmospheric base.
A prestigious central residential district of 1930s architecture and quiet tree-lined streets, popular with academics; suits those wanting a refined, calm, central neighborhood.

An insular ultra-Orthodox Haredi quarter with a 19th-century feel where modest dress is expected; suits culturally curious visitors wanting an authentic religious neighborhood while respecting local customs.
A charming maze of restored historic courtyard neighborhoods next to the Mahane Yehuda market, artsy and youthful; suits younger travelers and foodies wanting bohemian character near the market.
lodging: The Orient Jerusalem by Isrotel Exclusive Collection

water.note: Tap water meets high standards and is officially recommended by the Ministry of Health.

transit.pay: Use a rechargeable Rav-Kav smart card for both light rail and buses, or tap a contactless bank card directly on validators (increasingly accepted); buy/load Rav-Kav at kiosks, light-rail stations or online. A flat fare is about ILS 5.5 (~$1.50) with free transfers within 90 minutes.
transit.hours: Service runs Sunday-Thursday roughly 5:30am-midnight and a shortened Friday schedule before Shabbat; most lines pause Friday evening through Saturday and resume Saturday night.

transit.m: Train to Jerusalem Yitzhak Navon station, ~35 min
Nesher shared shuttle to any Jerusalem address, ~60-90 min

food.name: Hummus
food.desc: Warm, loose chickpea puree flooded with tahini and olive oil, topped with whole chickpeas or ful and mopped with pita - a breakfast, not a dip.

places.name: Abu Shukri
places.note: The Old City benchmark since the 1960s; hummus with pine nuts, ful and falafel, and nothing else on the table.

places.name: Lina Restaurant
places.note: Rival to Abu Shukri a few doors away; smoother, garlickier hummus and famously fast service.

places.name: Hummus Ben Sira
places.note: West Jerusalem favourite open late; masabacha and hummus with mushrooms for the after-dark crowd.

food.name: Meorav Yerushalmi
food.desc: The Jerusalem mixed grill: chicken hearts, livers and lamb offcuts seared on a flat-top with onion, cumin and turmeric, stuffed into pita or piled on rice.

places.name: Steakiyat Hatzot
places.note: One of several places claiming to have invented the dish; open very late, cash-friendly, unapologetically greasy.

places.name: Sima Restaurant
places.note: Neighbouring grill house with the same claim; generous portions, salads included, packed after midnight.

places.name: Mahane Yehuda grill stalls
places.note: Several market counters fire meorav to order at lunchtime - follow the smell and the queue.

food.name: Kubbeh soup
food.desc: Iraqi-Kurdish semolina dumplings stuffed with spiced minced beef, floating in beetroot, okra or hamusta sour-lemon broth - a Jerusalem market institution.

places.name: Morduch
places.note: Old-guard market restaurant; the beetroot kubbeh soup is the order, with stuffed vegetables alongside.

places.name: Azura
places.note: Kerosene-fired slow cooking since 1952; stuffed aubergine, oxtail and kubbeh, lunch only, no reservations.

places.name: Rachmo
places.note: Tiny, no-frills Kurdish kitchen serving kubbeh and hamusta to market traders since the 1930s.

food.name: Knafeh
food.desc: Shredded pastry or semolina over stretchy white cheese, baked orange, drowned in rose-scented syrup and scattered with pistachio - eaten hot from the tray.

places.name: Jafar Sweets
places.note: The Old City name for knafeh; trays cut in front of you and served on paper, best mid-afternoon.

places.name: Zalatimo Sweets
places.note: Century-old sweet shop also known for mutabbaq, a rarer layered cheese pastry.

places.name: Jafar Sweets, Salah al-Din
places.note: Larger branch on the main East Jerusalem shopping street with shorter queues than the Old City shop.

food.name: Rugelach
food.desc: Yeasted, chocolate-filled crescents baked dark and glazed with syrup while hot - Jerusalem's version is stickier and less buttery than the New York kind.

places.name: Marzipan Bakery
places.note: The rugelach people queue for; buy them warm, straight from the tray, and eat them the same day.

places.name: Teller Bakery
places.note: Long-running market bakery whose chocolate rugelach many locals rate above the more famous rival.

places.name: Kadosh Cafe
places.note: Patisserie-cafe doing a more refined rugelach with proper coffee and a sit-down room.

food.name: Malabi
food.desc: Cool, wobbly milk-and-cornflour pudding under rosewater syrup, shredded coconut and crushed peanuts, served in a plastic cup for a couple of shekels.

places.name: Mahane Yehuda dessert stalls
places.note: Several stalls scoop malabi to order; look for the trays of pink syrup and coconut on the counter.

places.name: Damascus Gate sweet vendors
places.note: Carts near the gate sell malabi and sahlab, especially in the cooler months.

places.name: Kadosh Cafe
places.note: Plated, dressed-up malabi if you would rather sit down than eat standing in the market.

food.name: Limonana
food.desc: Lemon and mint blitzed with ice into a pale green slush - the drink that gets everyone through a Jerusalem summer afternoon.

places.name: Mahane Yehuda juice stalls
places.note: Fresh-squeezed pomegranate, carrot and limonana from stalls throughout the market lanes.

places.name: Kadosh Cafe
places.note: Sit-down limonana with a pastry, on one of the pleasanter city-centre corners.

places.name: Old City juice carts
places.note: Carts along the market street press juice and mint lemonade to order in the shade of the arches.

food.name: Arabic coffee and sahlab
food.desc: Cardamom-heavy coffee poured thick from a long-spouted dallah, and sahlab, a hot milky orchid-root drink dusted with cinnamon and coconut in winter.

places.name: Austrian Hospice Cafe
places.note: Walled garden and rooftop above the Old City; Arabic coffee and apple strudel in unlikely combination.

places.name: Educational Bookshop Cafe
places.note: Bookshop cafe that is a calm place for Palestinian coffee and conversation away from the crowds.

places.name: Khan al-Zeit coffee vendors
places.note: Street vendors pour cardamom coffee and, in winter, sahlab from steaming urns along the market street.

landmarks: Western Wall (Kotel)
The last remnant of the Second Temple's retaining wall, and Judaism's holiest accessible prayer site, iconic for its ancient stones and daily worshippers.
Dome of the Rock
The golden-domed shrine atop the Temple Mount, one of the most recognizable and photographed silhouettes in the world.
Al-Aqsa Mosque
The silver-domed mosque on the Temple Mount, the third holiest site in Sunni Islam and a striking architectural counterpart to the Dome of the Rock.
Church of the Holy Sepulchre
Revered by many Christians as the site of Jesus's crucifixion and burial, its ancient stone facade draws pilgrims from around the world.
Tower of David (Jerusalem Citadel)
A medieval citadel beside Jaffa Gate whose ancient ramparts and tower are lit up nightly for a popular sound-and-light show.
Mount of Olives
A hillside cemetery and viewpoint east of the Old City offering the classic panoramic photograph of Jerusalem's skyline.
Via Dolorosa
The winding stone-paved route through the Old City traditionally believed to trace Jesus's path to crucifixion, lined with historic chapels and arches.
Garden of Gethsemane
An olive grove at the foot of the Mount of Olives associated with Jesus's final prayers, prized for its ancient gnarled trees.
City of David
An archaeological excavation site revealing Jerusalem's earliest settlement layers dating back roughly 3,000 years.
Yad Vashem
Israel's national Holocaust memorial and museum, notable for its striking modern architecture and moving memorial monuments.

train.note: Israel's rail network isn't connected to any neighbouring country, so there are no international trains. Israel Railways links Jerusalem's Yitzhak Navon station to Tel Aviv in about 35 minutes by fast electric train, and onward to Ben Gurion Airport and Haifa. Trains do not run on Shabbat (Friday evening to Saturday evening) or Jewish holidays.

bus.note: There are no through international coaches from Jerusalem. For Jordan you cross on foot at the Allenby / King Hussein Bridge (open in 2026) and pick up onward transport such as JETT buses on the Jordanian side; for Egypt travellers use the Taba crossing near Eilat. Domestic intercity buses are run mainly by Egged (https://www.egged.co.il/en) and pause on Shabbat and holidays. Check current security advice before using the land borders.

ferry.note: There is no scheduled international passenger ferry from Israel; Haifa handles cargo and cruise ships only. Proposed Haifa-Cyprus/Greece passenger services have not materialised as regular routes.

half.name: Dead Sea
half.blurb: Float effortlessly in the mineral-rich waters of Earth's lowest and saltiest lake.

half.name: Masada
half.blurb: This dramatic clifftop fortress overlooking the Dead Sea holds a legendary ancient siege story.

half.name: Bethlehem
half.blurb: Just south of Jerusalem lies the storied birthplace town revered across many faiths.

half.name: Ein Gedi
half.blurb: A lush desert oasis with waterfalls, springs and wildlife beside the Dead Sea.

half.name: Tel Aviv and Jaffa
half.blurb: Mediterranean beaches, buzzing nightlife and the ancient port quarter of Old Jaffa await.

half.name: Jericho
half.blurb: Explore one of the world's oldest inhabited cities in the Jordan Valley.
